The '''Ngarinyin''' language, also known as '''Ungarinjin''' and '''Eastern Worrorran''', is an [[endangered language|endangered]] [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]] of the [[Kimberley (Western Australia)|Kimberley]] region of [[Western Australia]] spoken by the [[Ngarinyin]] people.

==Classification and naming ==
Ngarinyin is one of the [[Worrorran languages]], along with [[Wunambal language|Wunambal]] and [[Worrorra language|(Western) Worrowan]].<ref name=bowern/>

It is itself a [[dialect cluster]], and may be considered more than a single language; [[Robert M. W. Dixon]] lists Guwidj (Orla), Waladja (Worla), Ngarnawu,<ref>{{AIATSIS|K52|Ngarnawu}}</ref> Andadjin, Munumburru, Wolyamidi, and Waladjangarri (Waladjangari<ref>{{AIATSIS|K24|Waladjangari}}</ref>) as dialects.<ref name=AIATSIS/> [[Claire Bowern]] (2011) lists Ngarinyin, Andajin, and Worla.<ref name=bowern>Bowern, Claire. 2011. "[http://anggarrgoon.wordpress.com/2011/12/23/how-many-languages-were-spoken-in-australia/ How Many Languages Were Spoken in Australia?]", ''Anggarrgoon: Australian languages on the web'', 23 December 2011 ([http://pamanyungan.sites.yale.edu/master-list-australian-languages-v12 corrected] 6 February 2012)</ref><ref name="Historical and Pama-Nyungan Lab 2012">{{cite web | title=Master List of Australian Languages, v1.2 | website=Historical and Pama-Nyungan Lab | date=6 February 2012 | url=https://pamanyungan.sites.yale.edu/master-list-australian-languages-v12 | access-date=7 November 2020}}</ref>

According to Rumsey, Ngarinyin may be applied to either the language or the people who speak it, whereas Ungarinyin only refers to the language. McGregor reported that "Ngarinyin has been chosen as the preferred language name" by the community.<ref name=AIATSIS/>

== Usage ==
With only 38 people recorded as speaking the language at home in the [[2016 Australian census]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://stat.data.abs.gov.au/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=ABS_C16_T09_SA|title=Census 2016, Language spoken at home by Sex (SA2+)|publisher=ABS|website=stat.data.abs.gov.au|language=en-au|access-date=2017-10-30|archive-date=26 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226044803/http://stat.data.abs.gov.au/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=ABS_C16_T09_SA|url-status=dead}}</ref> Ngarinyin is considered a critically endangered and currently  [[moribund language|moribund]] language, though there are efforts being made to documenting speech and grammar structures before it becomes extinct, including the specifics on the terms of the kinship system of the language.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

Ngarinyin is found only within the local region of [[Northern Kimberley|Northern Kimberley, Australia]], and other local languages are found in the surrounding region instead due to the small population of Ngarinyin speakers, including the [[Worrorran languages]] of [[Wunambal language|Wunambal]] and [[Worrorra language|Worrorra]]. Ngarinyin is found at the centre of the region, and the other Aboriginal languages in the area face similar levels of endangerment.  Ngarinyin was previously one of the most prevalent of the Aboriginal languages in Northern Kimberley, but it has since become a language known only by a small number of the elderly.<ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=40327769|title=The Classification of Languages in North and North-West Australia| last=Capell| first=Arthur| journal=Oceania| date=1 May 2017|volume=10|issue=3|pages=241–272|doi=10.1002/j.1834-4461.1940.tb00292.x}}</ref>

[[Australian Kriol language|Kriol]] is often used by younger generations instead of Ngarinyin, though some knowledge of the language is still retained by these people.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/ung|title=Ngarinyin|work=Ethnologue|access-date=2017-05-01}}</ref>

===Kinship terms===
Ngarinyin places great emphasis on the classification of family members and is similar to the neighbouring Aboriginal languages of Worrorra and Wunambal to the point of being virtually identical, though it is still considered unusual among those that study [[Aboriginal kinship|kinship systems]] of Aboriginal languages.<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=40332242|title=Kinship and Context among the Ngarinyin|first=Alan|last=Rumsey|date=1 January 1981|journal=Oceania|volume=51|issue=3|pages=181–192|doi=10.1002/j.1834-4461.1981.tb01448.x}}</ref> One of the most noticeable features of this system is the use of identical terms given to kin usually separated by generation level. For instance, the titles ''wife's brother'', ''wife's father'' and ''wife's father's father'' in English all share the same title of ''waiingi'' in Ngarinyin.
